rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3-4 - authors run their own distributed Tetis model (100 Monte Carlo runs, 1994-2015) over the Plana de Valencia Sur and calibrate it against observed evaporative index, groundwater levels from four wells and soil moisture. Q2: Section 4.2 and Figure 6 - mean annual recharge under flood irrigation (231 mm) exceeded that under drip (210 mm) by about 10%, higher in 16 of 20 years, with a cumulative difference of 449 mm; model output was compared with observed groundwater levels (Figure 4) and field evaporative index (Figure 3) in the study area. Q4: Section 3.2, Figure 5 and Section 5.1 - the model simulates soil water storage in wet and dry pixels, ETa and percolation, and the authors attribute the recharge difference to irrigation-driven soil moisture state and irrigation schedule (flood areas accommodate about 35% more rain on the day of rainfall; excess summer irrigation produces recharge on non-rainy days). Q6: Section 2 and 3.3.3 - results aggregated across 68 irrigation sectors (382 km2 of orchards, 913 km2 model domain), i.e., basin/district scale. Q7: Section 4.2, Figure 7 and Section 5.4 - the flood>drip recharge result holds in years with below-average precipitation and during the March-September irrigation season; in wet years and in autumn-winter drip recharge can exceed flood; authors restrict findings to their hydroclimatic (Mediterranean) conditions. Q8: Sections 5.2, 5.3 and 6 - no split-sample validation possible, increasing uncertainty of absolute recharge; soil moisture data came from outside the modeled area; splitting sectors into wet/dry pixels is a strong simplification limiting interpretation to sector scale; findings limited to the Mediterranean region. Q9: Figures 6-8 and Section 4.2 - results given as median, minimum and maximum across the 12 accepted parameterizations (boxplots, shaded bands), annual recharge ranges (drip 84-343 mm, flood 132-338 mm), and regression coefficients with standard errors in Table 2.
rows.notes: Modeling study; the flood-versus-drip recharge difference itself is not directly measured, but the model was calibrated against groundwater levels and field ETa estimates from the real system, so counted as own evidence. Q3 no: a single modeling method, calibration on several data types is not triangulation of the recharge result. Q5 no: one region, one crop (citrus). Q7 is borderline: precipitation wetness is partly a gradient, but the authors explicitly frame it as the condition determining when flood recharge exceeds drip recharge. The passage's mechanism (return flows) matches the study's explanation of excess flood irrigation sustaining recharge in summer.

notes: Full text available and complete. Study concerns surface drip versus flood irrigation in citrus orchards, Valencia, Spain, modeled 1994-2015 with multi-objective calibration.
